changes.current_line: Customers see an average uplift in authorization rates with Authorization Boost and Adaptive Acceptance.
changes.change: For platforms with low average order values whose pain is engineering maintenance, not revenue leakage, stop leading with the acceptance-rate slide. In its place, invite their engineers to build their own core flow (for a sitter platform, sitter pay) in our sandbox in the first week of the evaluation.
changes.why: The acceptance-rate slide drew silence from a buyer whose average booking is 38 dollars, while the deal turned only when the customer's engineer built a working sitter payment flow in our sandbox.

changes.current_line: Financial infrastructure to grow globally, in every currency.
changes.change: For engineering-led platforms, open with: "Payments shouldn't be a team": get your engineers off payments maintenance and unblock the roadmap it keeps pushing back. Use launching in new countries as the reason to act now, not as the headline. Test "Stop babysitting payments" as the headline for engineering buyers.
changes.why: The customer's pain was two engineers kept busy maintaining sitter payments and a roadmap item pushed three quarters in a row, and the customer described it in their own words ("Payments shouldn't be a team," "We want to stop babysitting this"), while expansion only set the deadline.

changes.current_line: Onboard, verify and pay out to sellers worldwide, in their local currency.
changes.change: For platforms that pay service providers, use the buyer's own word for the people they pay: "Onboard, verify and pay your sitters in their local currency, without a payments team." Say "sitter pay", not "payouts" or "marketplace", and do not promise a specific payout day.
changes.why: The marketplace capabilities landed with this buyer, but the customer says "sitter pay" and nobody there says "payouts," so the line works better in their words.

changes.change: For buyers switching from an existing payments setup, add a migration proof point ahead of generic customer stories: a named reference of comparable size that moved saved cards without losing them, plus a written answer on PayPal and Venmo. It must answer the question "who's done this at our size without losing cards?"
changes.why: The buyer's concern shifted to "what do we lose," and his requests for a comparable-size saved-card reference and a Venmo answer went unmet, so these migration risks were carried into delivery.
